**The Hilbert space and its norm.** Throughout this item $H\ne\{0\}$ is a nonzero complex Hilbert space, with pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and with the induced norm $\|\psi\|:=\sqrt{\langle\psi,\psi\rangle}$ ([[def-inner-product-norm]], [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]). A **vector** is an element of $H$, and a **unit vector** is a vector $\psi$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. The **unit sphere** of $H$ is
$$S(H):=\{\psi\in H:\|\psi\|=1\},$$
and the set of **nonzero vectors** is $H^{\times}:=H\setminus\{0\}$. The hypothesis $H\ne\{0\}$ says exactly that $H^{\times}$ is nonempty; then $S(H)$ is nonempty as well, since for every nonzero $\psi$ the vector $\psi/\|\psi\|$ has norm one, because $\|\psi\|>0$ and $\|\psi/\|\psi\|\,\|=|\|\psi\|^{-1}|\,\|\psi\|=1$.

**Rays.** For $\psi\in H^{\times}$ the **ray** of $\psi$ is
$$[\psi]:=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C,\ z\ne0\}\subseteq H^{\times}.$$
A **ray** of $H$ is a subset of the form $[\psi]$ for some nonzero $\psi$, and an element of a ray is called a **representative** of it. The set of rays
$$R(H):=\{[\psi]:\psi\in H^{\times}\}$$
is the **ray space** of $H$. Two nonzero vectors $\psi,\varphi$ are **ray-equivalent** when they lie in a common ray, that is, when $\varphi=z\psi$ for some nonzero complex number $z$. Ray equivalence is an equivalence relation on $H^{\times}$: it is reflexive with $z=1$, symmetric with $z^{-1}$, and transitive by multiplying scalars. Its classes are exactly the rays, so $R(H)$ is the quotient set of $H^{\times}$ by this relation, and every nonzero vector lies in exactly one ray.

**Normalization.** The **normalization map** is
$$\nu:H^{\times}\longrightarrow S(H),\qquad \nu(\psi):=\frac{\psi}{\|\psi\|},$$
where the right-hand side is the scalar multiple $\|\psi\|^{-1}\psi$; the displayed definition is meaningful because $\|\psi\|>0$ for $\psi\ne0$. The vector $\nu(\psi)$ is the **normalization** of $\psi$.

**Phases.** The **phase group** is
$$U(1):=\{\zeta\in\mathbb C:|\zeta|=1\}$$
([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]), and a **phase factor** is an element of $U(1)$. Two vectors $\psi,\varphi$ are **phase-equivalent** when $\varphi=\zeta\psi$ for some phase factor $\zeta$. The **phase action** of $U(1)$ on the unit sphere is the map
$$U(1)\times S(H)\longrightarrow S(H),\qquad (\zeta,\psi)\longmapsto\zeta\psi,$$
which is well defined because $\|\zeta\psi\|=|\zeta|\,\|\psi\|=\|\psi\|$ for $\zeta\in U(1)$ and $\psi\in S(H)$. Ray equivalence allows multiplication by an arbitrary nonzero complex scalar, while phase equivalence allows multiplication by a scalar of modulus one only; within a given ray the two notions coincide exactly on representatives of equal norm, and the precise statements are proved in the normalization lemma of this page.

**Scope.** This definition fixes the mathematical objects of the state space of a Hilbert space and their elementary vocabulary: nonzero vectors, unit vectors, rays, the ray space, the normalization map and the phase action. It introduces no topology or measure on $R(H)$, no dynamics and no physical interpretation, and it uses no choice principle. The identification of rays with preparations and of the unit sphere with their normalized representatives is the model assumption stated in the framework's state postulate, not part of this mathematical definition; the orbit structure of the phase action is analysed in the normalization lemma of this page.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

**Density operators.** Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space. A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a) ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). The **state space** of $H$ is the set of all density operators on $H$ and is denoted
$$D(H):=\{\rho:\rho\ \text{is a density operator on}\ H\}.$$
An element of $D(H)$ is called a **state** of $H$ in the mathematical sense fixed here.

**Pure states.** A state $\rho\in D(H)$ is **pure** when there is a unit vector $u\in S(H)$ with
$$\rho=T_{u,u},\qquad T_{u,u}x=\langle x,u\rangle u\quad(x\in H),$$
where $T_{u,u}$ is the rank-one operator of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] and $S(H)$ is the unit sphere of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. By [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] the pure states are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range, and the map
$$j:R(H)\longrightarrow D(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
on the ray space $R(H)$, with $\nu$ the normalization map, is well defined and injective with image the set of pure states. A state is **mixed** when it is not pure. For a nonzero vector $\psi$ the **normalized rank-one operator of $\psi$** is
$$\widehat\rho(\psi):=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})},$$
which equals $T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)}$; thus $\widehat\rho(\psi)$ is the pure state of the ray $[\psi]$, and the vector $\psi$ enters only through its ray.

**Purity.** For $\rho\in D(H)$ the operator $\rho^{2}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class: it is self-adjoint by the adjoint algebra of [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], positive because $\langle\rho^{2}x,x\rangle=\langle\rho x,\rho x\rangle\ge0$, and trace class because $\rho$ is a bounded trace-class operator and the trace-class operators form a two-sided ideal ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]] clauses 1 and 2). The **purity** of $\rho$ is the real number
$$\mathcal P(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})\in\mathbb R.$$
The numerical range of the purity and the equivalence of purity with purity of the state are established by the purity criterion of this page; this definition records the object only.

**Scope.** This definition fixes the mathematical state space of a Hilbert space together with the pure states, the mixed states, the normalized rank-one operator of a nonzero vector and the purity functional. The cited rank-one calculus and the density-operator expansion assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and the definition is read under that assumption. It asserts no dynamics, no measurement, no probability law and no physical interpretation, and it introduces no new assumptions beyond the cited mathematics and that choice hypothesis. In particular, whether a given physical preparation is described by a pure or a mixed state is a question about the model's assignments, not about this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $V$ be a normed space. A **sequence in $V$** is a function
$x:\mathbb N\to V$, written $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_n:=x(n)$
([[def-natural-numbers]]). Fix such a sequence.

Define its vector partial sums recursively by

$$s_0:=0_V,\qquad s_{m+1}:=s_m+x_m.$$

We write $s_m=\sum_{n<m}x_n$. The **series**
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty x_n$ **converges** when these partial sums converge in $V$.
Its sum is then the limit of the partial sums.

The series is **absolutely convergent** when the scalar series
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \|x_n\|$$
converges in the sense of [[def-series]].

Let $V$ be a normed space in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$. Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A **sequence in $X$** is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$, written $(x_k)$ with
$x_k := x(k)$. As everywhere in this library, $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]) and a sequence is indexed from $0$
([[def-sequence]]); an index range copied from a text that starts at $1$ must be
shifted before it is used here.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence in $X$ and $p \in X$. The function
$k \mapsto d(x_k, p)$ is a sequence of reals ([[def-sequence]]), and it is
nonnegative ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]), so $|d(x_k,p)| = d(x_k,p)$
([[def-abs-value]]). Define

$$x_k \longrightarrow p \text{ in } (X,d) \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad d(x_k,p) \longrightarrow 0 \text{ in } \mathbb{R},$$

the convergence on the right being that of [[def-real-limit]]. Unwound, this
says: for every **rational** $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$d(x_k, p) < \varepsilon$ for every $k \ge K$. We then call $p$ a **limit** of
$(x_k)$, and say $(x_k)$ **converges** in $(X,d)$ if it has a limit.

**Rational and real $\varepsilon$ agree here, as they do on the real line.**
[[def-real-limit]] tests convergence against rational $\varepsilon$ only, and its
own remark, restated for sequences in [[def-sequence]], records that nothing is
lost: below any real $\eta > 0$ lies a positive rational
([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), and the index belonging to that rational serves for
$\eta$. So a proof may establish convergence by producing an index for every
real $\varepsilon > 0$, and may use a convergence hypothesis at a real
$\varepsilon$ by first passing to a rational below it. Both moves are used on
this page and are always cited.

**Subsequences and subsequential limits.** A **subsequence** of $(x_k)$ is the
composite $x \circ n$ for a strictly increasing $n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
written $(x_{n_j})$, exactly as for sequences of reals ([[def-sequence]]); and
$p$ is a **subsequential limit** of $(x_k)$ in $(X,d)$ when some subsequence
converges to $p$, which is the metric-space form of [[def-subsequential-limit]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

$(X,d)$ is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$
([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]) converges to a point of $X$
([[def-metric-convergence]]).

A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called **complete** when the metric subspace
$(A, d_A)$ is complete ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); as always, the
metric is part of the data, and $d_A$ is the restriction of $d$ to $A \times A$.

**The limit is unique when it exists**, since limits in a metric space are unique
([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]), so a complete space assigns to each of its Cauchy
sequences one point and not a set of points.

**Completeness is a property of the pair $(X,d)$, not of $X$ and not of the
topology of $d$.** Both quantifiers in the definition are about the metric: the
Cauchy condition is stated with distances, and so is convergence. Two metrics on
the same set can have the same open sets while exactly one of them is complete,
which is the content of [[fs-completeness-is-a-topological-property]] and its
witness. Read the word *complete* as an abbreviation for *complete with respect
to this metric*, always.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$
carry the subspace metric $d_A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). Then:

1. **Under countable choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]),
   if $(A,d_A)$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]), then $A$ is closed
   in $(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-topology]]). No completeness hypothesis on $X$ is needed.
2. **In ZF, without a choice axiom**, if $(X,d)$ is complete and $A$ is closed
   in $(X,d)$, then $(A,d_A)$ is complete.

Consequently, under countable choice, a subspace of a complete metric space is
complete if and only if it is closed.

The following form of the first direction is also choice-free: a complete
subspace contains the ambient limit of every convergent sequence of its
points. Hence it is closed whenever every point of its ambient closure is
already known to be the limit of a sequence from that subspace. This last
condition is pointwise existence, not a chosen family of sequences.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]).

1. $F$ is a vector space over itself ([[def-vector-space]]): take the set to be
   $F$, the vector addition to be the field addition, the zero vector to be
   $0_F$, and the scalar multiplication $F \times F \to F$ to be the field
   multiplication.
2. Let $K \subseteq F$ be a subfield ([[def-subfield]]) and let $V$ be a vector
   space over $F$. Then $V$, with the same addition and the same zero vector and
   with the scalar multiplication restricted to $K \times V$, is a vector space
   over $K$. This is called **restricting the scalars** from $F$ to $K$.
3. In particular $F$ is a vector space over every subfield $K \subseteq F$, with
   the field multiplication restricted to $K \times F$ as scalar multiplication.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), regarded as a commutative ring by
[[lem-field-is-a-commutative-ring]]. A subset $K \subseteq F$ is a **subfield**
of $F$ when

- **(K1)** $K$ is a subring of $F$ ([[def-subring]]);
- **(K2)** $x^{-1} \in K$ for every $x \in K$ with $x \ne 0_F$.

Equivalently, by [[lem-subring-criterion]], $K$ is a subfield exactly when
$1_F \in K$, $a - b \in K$ and $ab \in K$ for all $a, b \in K$, and
$x^{-1} \in K$ for every nonzero $x \in K$.

**Why $K$ is then a field, and with the same $0$ and $1$.** By (K1) and
[[def-subring]], $K$ with the restricted operations is a ring whose zero is
$0_F$ and whose identity is $1_F$; its multiplication is commutative, being the
restriction of a commutative one ([[def-commutative-ring]]). Since $1_F \ne 0_F$
in $F$ and both lie in $K$, we have $1_K \ne 0_K$. Let $x \in K$ with
$x \ne 0_K$; then $x \ne 0_F$, so $x^{-1} \in F$ exists and lies in $K$ by (K2),
and $x x^{-1} = 1_F = 1_K = x^{-1} x$. So every nonzero element of $K$ is a unit
of the ring $K$, and $K$ is a commutative division ring ([[def-division-ring]]);
by [[lem-commutative-division-ring-is-a-field]] it is a field. Moreover the
inverse of $x$ computed in $K$ is its inverse computed in $F$, since $x^{-1}$
already satisfies the defining equation inside $K$.

In particular

$$0_K = 0_F, \qquad 1_K = 1_F, \qquad (-x)_K = (-x)_F, \qquad (x^{-1})_K = (x^{-1})_F \quad (x \in K,\ x \ne 0_F).$$

**A subfield of an ordered field inherits the order.** Let $(F,P)$ be an ordered
field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $K$ a subfield. Put $P_K := P \cap K$. Then
(O1) holds in $K$: for $x \in K$ we have $-x \in K$ by (K1), and exactly one of
$x \in P$, $x = 0_F$, $-x \in P$ holds in $F$, so exactly one of
$x \in P_K$, $x = 0_K$, $-x \in P_K$ holds. And (O2) holds: if $x, y \in P_K$
then $x + y$ and $xy$ lie in $P$ by (O2) in $F$ and in $K$ by (K1), hence in
$P_K$. So $(K,P_K)$ is an ordered field, and its order is the restriction of the
order of $F$, because $a < b$ means $b - a \in P$ on both sides and
$b - a$ is the same element in $K$ as in $F$.

derivations.claim: [(a) finite mixtures are states] Let $\rho,\sigma\in D(H)$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$ real. The combination $\lambda\rho+(1-\lambda)\sigma$ is trace class by [F1] and self-adjoint because $(\lambda\rho+(1-\lambda)\sigma)^{*}=\lambda\rho^{*}+(1-\lambda)\sigma^{*}=\lambda\rho+(1-\lambda)\sigma$ by [F4] with real scalars; it is positive because $\langle(\lambda\rho+(1-\lambda)\sigma)x,x\rangle=\lambda\langle\rho x,x\rangle+(1-\lambda)\langle\sigma x,x\rangle\ge0$ by [F2] and [F3]; and its trace is $\lambda\operatorname{tr}\rho+(1-\lambda)\operatorname{tr}\sigma=\lambda+(1-\lambda)=1$ by the linearity of the trace in [F3]. Hence it is a density operator, so $D(H)$ is closed under finite real convex combinations in the reading of [F8]; the finite-combination statement follows by induction on the number of components.

[(b) the mixture series converges in the trace norm] For every $n$ the operator $w_n\rho_n$ is self-adjoint by [F4] and positive, and it is trace class with $\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=w_n\|\rho_n\|_1=w_n\operatorname{tr}\rho_n=w_n$ by [F1] and [F3]; hence $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=\sum_nw_n=1<\infty$, so the series is absolutely convergent in the Banach space $\mathcal S_1(H)$ by [F6] and has a trace-class sum $T$; moreover $\|T-\sum_{n<K}w_n\rho_n\|_1\to0$ because the tail is a convergent series of norms of the omitted terms, by [F6]. The self-adjointness argument below places this sum in $X$.

[(a) $X$ is a real Banach space] If $T_m\in X$ and $\|T_m-T\|_1\to0$, then by [F1] and [F4], $\|T^{*}-T\|\le\|T^{*}-T_m^{*}\|+\|T_m-T\|=\|(T_m-T)^{*}\|+\|T_m-T\|=2\|T_m-T\|\le2\|T_m-T\|_1\to0$. Thus $T^{*}=T$ and $X$ is closed in $\mathcal S_1(H)$. It is a real-linear subspace because sums and real scalar multiples of self-adjoint operators are self-adjoint by [F4], and it is complete in the restricted trace-norm metric by [F7] applied to the complete space $\mathcal S_1(H)$ of [F1].

[(c) block members are states] Fix $k$ with $u_k>0$. The finite combination $\sigma_k=u_k^{-1}\sum_{N_k\le n<N_{k+1}}w_n\rho_n$ is a convex combination of the operators $\rho_n$, $N_k\le n<N_{k+1}$, with nonnegative real coefficients $w_n/u_k$ summing to $1$ (the finite sum of the weights is $u_k$), so $\sigma_k\in D(H)$ by step 1.1 and induction.

[(b) the mixture sum is a state] Let $S_K:=\sum_{n<K}w_n\rho_n$, the self-adjoint partial sums of step 1.2. Trace-norm convergence and [F1] give $\|T-S_K\|\to0$, and operator-norm continuity of the adjoint [F4] gives $\|T^{*}-T\|\le\|T^{*}-S_K^{*}\|+\|S_K-T\|=2\|T-S_K\|\le2\|T-S_K\|_1\to0$. Hence $T$ is self-adjoint. It is positive because for every $x$ the numbers $\langle S_Kx,x\rangle=\sum_{n<K}w_n\langle\rho_nx,x\rangle$ are nonnegative by [F2], while $|\langle(T-S_K)x,x\rangle|\le\|T-S_K\|_1\|x\|^{2}\to0$ by [F5], so $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$; and $\operatorname{tr}T=\lim_K\sum_{n<K}w_n=1$ because $|\operatorname{tr}T-\operatorname{tr}S_K|\le\|T-S_K\|_1\to0$ by [F3] and the trace is linear. Thus $T\in D(H)\subseteq X$, and since $S_K\in X$ this trace-norm convergence is also convergence in $X$.

[(c) grouping of consecutive blocks] Let $T_m:=\sum_{n<m}w_n\rho_n$ be the partial sums of the $n$-series; by regrouping finite sums in the real vector space $X$ one has, for every $K$, $\sum_{k<K}u_k\sigma_k=\sum_{k<K}\sum_{N_k\le n<N_{k+1}}w_n\rho_n=\sum_{n<N_K}w_n\rho_n=T_{N_K}.$ Since $T_m\to T$ by step 1.2 and $N_K\to\infty$, the sequence $(T_{N_K})_K$ is a subsequence of a convergent sequence in the metric space $X$ and therefore converges to $T$ as well by [F6]; the left series converges absolutely because $\sum_k\|u_k\sigma_k\|_1=\sum_ku_k\operatorname{tr}\sigma_k=\sum_ku_k=\sum_nw_n=1$ by [F3] and step 2.1. Hence both series have the same sum $T$.

[(d) closedness and completeness] Let $\rho_m\in D(H)$ converge to $\rho\in X$ in the trace norm. Then $\rho$ is self-adjoint by definition of $X$; it is positive because $|\langle(\rho-\rho_m)x,x\rangle|\le\|\rho-\rho_m\|_1\|x\|^{2}\to0$ by [F5] while $\langle\rho_mx,x\rangle\ge0$; and $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\lim_m\operatorname{tr}\rho_m=1$ by [F3] and trace linearity. Hence $\rho\in D(H)$, so $D(H)$ is closed in $X$; since $X$ is complete by step 1.3, $D(H)$ is complete for the restricted metric by [F7]. This proves (a)-(d).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

**Density operators.** Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space. A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a) ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). The **state space** of $H$ is the set of all density operators on $H$ and is denoted
$$D(H):=\{\rho:\rho\ \text{is a density operator on}\ H\}.$$
An element of $D(H)$ is called a **state** of $H$ in the mathematical sense fixed here.

**Pure states.** A state $\rho\in D(H)$ is **pure** when there is a unit vector $u\in S(H)$ with
$$\rho=T_{u,u},\qquad T_{u,u}x=\langle x,u\rangle u\quad(x\in H),$$
where $T_{u,u}$ is the rank-one operator of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] and $S(H)$ is the unit sphere of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. By [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] the pure states are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range, and the map
$$j:R(H)\longrightarrow D(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
on the ray space $R(H)$, with $\nu$ the normalization map, is well defined and injective with image the set of pure states. A state is **mixed** when it is not pure. For a nonzero vector $\psi$ the **normalized rank-one operator of $\psi$** is
$$\widehat\rho(\psi):=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})},$$
which equals $T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)}$; thus $\widehat\rho(\psi)$ is the pure state of the ray $[\psi]$, and the vector $\psi$ enters only through its ray.

**Purity.** For $\rho\in D(H)$ the operator $\rho^{2}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class: it is self-adjoint by the adjoint algebra of [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], positive because $\langle\rho^{2}x,x\rangle=\langle\rho x,\rho x\rangle\ge0$, and trace class because $\rho$ is a bounded trace-class operator and the trace-class operators form a two-sided ideal ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]] clauses 1 and 2). The **purity** of $\rho$ is the real number
$$\mathcal P(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})\in\mathbb R.$$
The numerical range of the purity and the equivalence of purity with purity of the state are established by the purity criterion of this page; this definition records the object only.

**Scope.** This definition fixes the mathematical state space of a Hilbert space together with the pure states, the mixed states, the normalized rank-one operator of a nonzero vector and the purity functional. The cited rank-one calculus and the density-operator expansion assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and the definition is read under that assumption. It asserts no dynamics, no measurement, no probability law and no physical interpretation, and it introduces no new assumptions beyond the cited mathematics and that choice hypothesis. In particular, whether a given physical preparation is described by a pure or a mixed state is a question about the model's assignments, not about this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, which is the choice hypothesis of the rank-one calculus [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$$T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u\qquad(x\in H)$$
be the rank-one operator calculus of that item. Use the notation of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]] for the unit sphere $S(H)$, the nonzero vectors $H^{\times}$, the ray $[\psi]$, the ray space $R(H)$ and the normalization $\nu$. Then:

(a) For every $\psi\in H^{\times}$ the operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ is a nonzero self-adjoint positive trace-class operator with
$$\|T_{\psi,\psi}\|_1=\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})=\|\psi\|^{2},\qquad T_{\psi,\psi}=\|\psi\|^{2}\,T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},\qquad \langle T_{\psi,\psi}x,x\rangle=|\langle x,\psi\rangle|^{2}\quad(x\in H).$$

(b) For every $u\in S(H)$ the operator $T_{u,u}$ is the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto the one-dimensional linear subspace $\mathbb Cu$; in particular $T_{u,u}\ne0$, $T_{u,u}^{2}=T_{u,u}$ and $T_{u,u}^{*}=T_{u,u}$. Conversely, if $M$ is a one-dimensional linear subspace of $H$ and $u\in S(H)$ satisfies $M=\mathbb Cu$, then the Hilbert orthogonal projection $P_M$ onto $M$ equals $T_{u,u}$. Thus the operators $T_{u,u}$ with $u\in S(H)$ are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range.

(c) For nonzero $\psi,\varphi\in H^{\times}$:
$$T_{\psi,\psi}=T_{\varphi,\varphi}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \|\psi\|=\|\varphi\|\ \text{and}\ [\psi]=[\varphi].$$
In particular, for $u,w\in S(H)$ one has $T_{u,u}=T_{w,w}$ if and only if $w=\zeta u$ for some $\zeta\in U(1)$.

(d) The map
$$j:R(H)\longrightarrow \mathcal S_1(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
is well defined and injective, and its image is exactly $\{T_{u,u}:u\in S(H)\}$.

derivations.claim: [(a) the weights are positive and sum to one] By [F1] the $\lambda_n$ are exactly the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity, so $\lambda_n>0$ for $n\in J$; the identity $\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ is [F1] together with [F3] applied to the positive trace-class operator $\rho$; since all terms are nonnegative and their sum is $1$, each single term satisfies $\lambda_n\le1$.

[(b) the eigenvalues of $\rho^{2}$] By [F4] and [F5] the operator $\rho^{2}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class. For $x\in H$ the spectral expansion of [F2] gives $\rho x=\sum_{n}\lambda_nP_nx$ with $P_nx\in E_{\lambda_n}$; applying $\rho$ to this norm-convergent series and using $\rho P_nx=\lambda_nP_nx$ gives $\rho^{2}x=\sum_{n}\lambda_n^{2}P_nx$, the series converging in norm because $\sum_n\lambda_n^{2}\|P_nx\|^{2}\le\sum_n\lambda_n\|P_nx\|^{2}\le\|x\|^{2}$ by $\lambda_n\le1$ and the expansion of $x$ in the orthogonal family $(E_{\lambda_n})\oplus\ker\rho$. If now $\rho^{2}x=\mu x$ with $\mu>0$ and $x\ne0$, then $x\in\operatorname{ran}(\rho^{2})\subseteq\operatorname{ran}\rho\subseteq \overline{\operatorname{ran}\rho}=M$ by [F2]; so [F6] expands $x=\sum_n\langle x,u_n\rangle u_n$ in the complete orthonormal family $(u_n)$ of $M$, and comparing coefficients in the two expansions of $\rho^{2}x$ by the uniqueness clause of [F6] gives $(\lambda_n^{2}-\mu)\langle x,u_n\rangle=0$ for every $n$. Hence every nonzero coefficient has $\lambda_n^{2}=\mu$, so the positive eigenvalues of $\rho^{2}$ are exactly the numbers $\lambda_n^{2}$ with multiplicity, and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})=\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n^{2}$ by [F3]. The sum is positive because some $\lambda_n>0$ by $\sum\lambda_n=1$, and it is at most $1$ because $\lambda_n^{2}\le\lambda_n$ by step 1.1 and $\sum\lambda_n=1$.

[(c) equivalences] Statement (i) holds, that is $\sum_n\lambda_n^{2}=1=\sum_n\lambda_n$, if and only if $\sum_n\lambda_n(1-\lambda_n)=0$; since $0\le\lambda_n\le1$ by step 1.1, each term is nonnegative, so this happens exactly when $\lambda_n\in\{0,1\}$ for every $n$, and because $\lambda_n>0$ on the index set $J$ and $\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n=1$, exactly when $J$ consists of a single index $n_0$ with $\lambda_{n_0}=1$; this is (ii). If (ii) holds, then the expansion of [F1] reads $\rho=T_{u_{n_0},u_{n_0}}$ with $u_{n_0}$ a unit vector of the orthonormal family, so $\rho$ is pure, which is (iii), by [F7]. If $\rho$ is pure, say $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$, then $\rho^{2}=\rho$ by the product rule $T_{u,u}T_{u,u}=T_{T_{u,u}u,u}=T_{u,u}$ recalled in [F7], giving (iv). Finally, if $\rho^{2}=\rho$ and $\rho x=\lambda x$, then $\lambda^{2}x=\rho^{2}x=\rho x=\lambda x$, so $\lambda\in\{0,1\}$ for the positive eigenvalues $n\in J$; since their sum is $1$ there is exactly one index $n_0$ with $\lambda_{n_0}=1$, which is (ii), and then $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ gives (i). The implications (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii)$\Rightarrow$(iv)$\Rightarrow$(ii) show that all four statements are equivalent.

[(d) non-pure states have at least two positive eigenvalues] If $\rho$ is not pure, then $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})\ne1$ by step 3.1, and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})\le1$ by step 2.1, so $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})<1$. If $J$ had exactly one index $n_0$, then $\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n=\lambda_{n_0}=1$ by step 1.1, and condition (ii) of step 3.1 would hold, making $\rho$ pure by that step, a contradiction; hence $J$ has at least two indices. This proves (a)-(d).

boundaries.evidence: The index set J is nonempty because Σλ_n=1 by step 1.1; the finite case is the stated zero-padding convention.
Zero eigenvalues and the zero-padding beyond a finite index set are handled in step 2.1, and the equality analysis of step 3.1 uses λ_n∈{0,1}.
The single-index case J={n_0} with λ_{n_0}=1 is exactly condition (ii) proved equivalent in step 3.1.

boundaries.reason: No degenerate limit or coincident case occurs; multiplicities are treated by counting eigenvalues with multiplicity throughout.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 treats the extreme purity value one through the positive eigenweights summing to one; the zero/one eigenweight alternatives are used in its equality criterion.
The statement declares the Axiom of Countable Choice; it is used through the spectral and trace suppliers invoked in steps 2.1 and 3.1.
The chain (i)⟹(ii)⟹(iii)⟹(iv)⟹(ii) is proved in step 3.1, with the final step closing the cycle.
The implications in the reverse directions are the same display in step 3.1 read backwards (equivalence of all four conditions).

**Pure states.** A state $\rho\in D(H)$ is **pure** when there is a unit vector $u\in S(H)$ with
$$\rho=T_{u,u},\qquad T_{u,u}x=\langle x,u\rangle u\quad(x\in H),$$
where $T_{u,u}$ is the rank-one operator of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] and $S(H)$ is the unit sphere of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. By [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] the pure states are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range, and the map
$$j:R(H)\longrightarrow D(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
on the ray space $R(H)$, with $\nu$ the normalization map, is well defined and injective with image the set of pure states. A state is **mixed** when it is not pure. For a nonzero vector $\psi$ the **normalized rank-one operator of $\psi$** is
$$\widehat\rho(\psi):=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})},$$
which equals $T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)}$; thus $\widehat\rho(\psi)$ is the pure state of the ray $[\psi]$, and the vector $\psi$ enters only through its ray.

**Purity.** For $\rho\in D(H)$ the operator $\rho^{2}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class: it is self-adjoint by the adjoint algebra of [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], positive because $\langle\rho^{2}x,x\rangle=\langle\rho x,\rho x\rangle\ge0$, and trace class because $\rho$ is a bounded trace-class operator and the trace-class operators form a two-sided ideal ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]] clauses 1 and 2). The **purity** of $\rho$ is the real number
$$\mathcal P(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})\in\mathbb R.$$
The numerical range of the purity and the equivalence of purity with purity of the state are established by the purity criterion of this page; this definition records the object only.

**Scope.** This definition fixes the mathematical state space of a Hilbert space together with the pure states, the mixed states, the normalized rank-one operator of a nonzero vector and the purity functional. The cited rank-one calculus and the density-operator expansion assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and the definition is read under that assumption. It asserts no dynamics, no measurement, no probability law and no physical interpretation, and it introduces no new assumptions beyond the cited mathematics and that choice hypothesis. In particular, whether a given physical preparation is described by a pure or a mixed state is a question about the model's assignments, not about this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $\rho\in D(H)$ be a density operator ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). Let
$$(\lambda_n)_{n\in J},\qquad J\ \text{a finite initial segment of}\ \mathbb N\ \text{or all of}\ \mathbb N,$$
be the positive eigenvalues of $\rho$ listed with multiplicity, so that $\rho=\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ for an orthonormal family $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ of eigenvectors, $\rho u_n=\lambda_nu_n$ ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]). Then:

(a) $\lambda_n>0$ for every $n\in J$, $\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n=1$, and $\lambda_n\le1$ for every $n\in J$.

(b) $\rho^{2}$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator, and its positive eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are exactly the numbers $\lambda_n^{2}$ with $n\in J$; consequently
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})=\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n^{2}\in(0,1].$$

(c) The following four statements are equivalent: (i) $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})=1$; (ii) $J=\{n_0\}$ for a single index $n_0$ and $\lambda_{n_0}=1$; (iii) $\rho$ is a pure state; (iv) $\rho^{2}=\rho$.

(d) If $\rho$ is not pure, then $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})<1$ and $J$ contains at least two indices, so that $\rho$ has at least two positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $D(H)$ be the state space of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]. Write $\mathcal S_1(H)$ for the complex Banach space of trace-class operators on $H$ with the trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$, and
$$X:=\{\rho\in\mathcal S_1(H):\rho^{*}=\rho\}$$
for the set of self-adjoint trace-class operators, regarded as a real vector space by restricting scalars from $\mathbb C$ to $\mathbb R$ ([[lem-restriction-of-scalars]], [[def-subfield]]). Then:

(a) **Finite mixtures.** $X$ is a closed real-linear subspace of $\mathcal S_1(H)$ and hence a real Banach space, and $D(H)\subseteq X$ is **closed under finite real convex combinations**, that is, it contains with any two of its points the whole real segment between them: for all $\rho,\sigma\in D(H)$ and every real $\lambda\in[0,1]$,
$$\lambda\rho+(1-\lambda)\sigma\in D(H).$$
By induction every finite convex combination $\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_j\rho_j$ with $\rho_j\in D(H)$, real $\lambda_j\ge0$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j=1$ is again an element of $D(H)$.

(b) **Countable mixtures.** Let $(\rho_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq D(H)$ and let $(w_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be real weights with $w_n\ge0$ and $\sum_{n}w_n=1$. Then the series $\sum_{n}w_n\rho_n$ converges absolutely in $\|\cdot\|_1$ to an element of $D(H)$: the series converges in $X$, its sum $T$ satisfies $T^{*}=T$, $T\ge0$, $\operatorname{tr}T=1$, and $\|T\|_1=\operatorname{tr}T$, with
$$\Bigl\|T-\sum_{n<K}w_n\rho_n\Bigr\|_1\longrightarrow0\quad(K\to\infty).$$

(c) **Grouping of consecutive blocks.** In the situation of (b) let $0=N_0<N_1<N_2<\cdots$ be an increasing sequence with $N_k\to\infty$, and for every $k\in\mathbb N$ put
$$u_k:=\sum_{N_k\le n<N_{k+1}}w_n,\qquad \sigma_k:=\frac{1}{u_k}\sum_{N_k\le n<N_{k+1}}w_n\rho_n,$$
where it is assumed that $u_k>0$ for every $k$ (blocks of zero weight are omitted). Then $\sigma_k\in D(H)$ for every $k$, $\sum_ku_k=1$, and
$$\sum_{k}u_k\sigma_k=\sum_{n}w_n\rho_n$$
in $\|\cdot\|_1$, the series on the left converging absolutely.

(d) **Closedness and completeness.** $D(H)$ is closed in the Banach space $(X,\|\cdot\|_1)$, and $D(H)$ is complete for the trace-norm metric.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, which is the choice hypothesis of the rank-one calculus [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$$T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u\qquad(x\in H)$$
be the rank-one operator calculus of that item. Use the notation of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]] for the unit sphere $S(H)$, the nonzero vectors $H^{\times}$, the ray $[\psi]$, the ray space $R(H)$ and the normalization $\nu$. Then:

(a) For every $\psi\in H^{\times}$ the operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ is a nonzero self-adjoint positive trace-class operator with
$$\|T_{\psi,\psi}\|_1=\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})=\|\psi\|^{2},\qquad T_{\psi,\psi}=\|\psi\|^{2}\,T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},\qquad \langle T_{\psi,\psi}x,x\rangle=|\langle x,\psi\rangle|^{2}\quad(x\in H).$$

(b) For every $u\in S(H)$ the operator $T_{u,u}$ is the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto the one-dimensional linear subspace $\mathbb Cu$; in particular $T_{u,u}\ne0$, $T_{u,u}^{2}=T_{u,u}$ and $T_{u,u}^{*}=T_{u,u}$. Conversely, if $M$ is a one-dimensional linear subspace of $H$ and $u\in S(H)$ satisfies $M=\mathbb Cu$, then the Hilbert orthogonal projection $P_M$ onto $M$ equals $T_{u,u}$. Thus the operators $T_{u,u}$ with $u\in S(H)$ are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range.

(c) For nonzero $\psi,\varphi\in H^{\times}$:
$$T_{\psi,\psi}=T_{\varphi,\varphi}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \|\psi\|=\|\varphi\|\ \text{and}\ [\psi]=[\varphi].$$
In particular, for $u,w\in S(H)$ one has $T_{u,u}=T_{w,w}$ if and only if $w=\zeta u$ for some $\zeta\in U(1)$.

(d) The map
$$j:R(H)\longrightarrow \mathcal S_1(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
is well defined and injective, and its image is exactly $\{T_{u,u}:u\in S(H)\}$.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]).

1. $F$ is a vector space over itself ([[def-vector-space]]): take the set to be
   $F$, the vector addition to be the field addition, the zero vector to be
   $0_F$, and the scalar multiplication $F \times F \to F$ to be the field
   multiplication.
2. Let $K \subseteq F$ be a subfield ([[def-subfield]]) and let $V$ be a vector
   space over $F$. Then $V$, with the same addition and the same zero vector and
   with the scalar multiplication restricted to $K \times V$, is a vector space
   over $K$. This is called **restricting the scalars** from $F$ to $K$.
3. In particular $F$ is a vector space over every subfield $K \subseteq F$, with
   the field multiplication restricted to $K \times F$ as scalar multiplication.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

**Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

**Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

derivations.claim: [(pure $\Rightarrow$ extreme) the quadratic forms are pinned to one] Assume $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $u\in S(H)$ and $\rho=(1-t)\sigma+t\tau$ with $0<t<1$. Then $\langle\rho u,u\rangle=\langle T_{u,u}u,u\rangle=\langle u,u\rangle^{2}=\|u\|^{2}=1$ by [F5] and the definition of $T_{u,u}$, so $1=(1-t)\langle\sigma u,u\rangle+t\langle\tau u,u\rangle$. Every state $\eta\in D(H)$ satisfies $\langle\eta u,u\rangle\ge0$ by positivity and $\langle\eta u,u\rangle\le|\langle\eta u,u\rangle|\le\|\eta u\|\,\|u\|=\|\eta u\|\le\|\eta\|\le\|\eta\|_1=1$ by [F4]; a real convex combination with weights $1-t,t>0$ of two numbers $\le1$ equals $1$ only if both numbers equal $1$. Hence $\langle\sigma u,u\rangle=\langle\tau u,u\rangle=1$.

[(pure $\Rightarrow$ extreme) the first component fixes $u$] For the state $\sigma$ we have the chain $1=\langle\sigma u,u\rangle\le|\langle\sigma u,u\rangle|\le\|\sigma u\|\,\|u\|=\|\sigma u\|\le\|\sigma\|\le1$ by [F4]; all inequalities are therefore equalities, so equality holds in the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the pair $(\sigma u,u)$, and the equality case of [F4] gives $\sigma u=\zeta u$ for a scalar $\zeta$ because $u\ne0$. Taking the pairing with $u$ gives $1=\langle\sigma u,u\rangle=\zeta\langle u,u\rangle=\zeta$, so $\sigma u=u$. The same argument gives $\tau u=u$.

[(pure $\Rightarrow$ extreme) a state fixing $u$ equals $T_{u,u}$] Let $\eta\in D(H)$ with $\eta u=u$. By [F3] the positive eigenvalues $\lambda_n$ of $\eta$, counted with multiplicity, satisfy $\sum_n\lambda_n=1$, and $u$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $1$: $u\in E_1(\eta)$. If $m$ denotes the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $1$, that is the number of indices with $\lambda_n=1$, then $1=\sum_n\lambda_n=m+\sum_{\lambda_n\ne1}\lambda_n$ with a nonnegative second sum, so $m=1$ and there is no other positive eigenvalue; hence $E_1(\eta)=\mathbb Cu$ and the spectral expansion of [F3] reads $\eta x=P_1x$ for every $x$, where $P_1$ is the orthogonal projection onto $E_1(\eta)=\mathbb Cu$. By [F7] and [F5] the projection onto $\mathbb Cu$ is $T_{u,u}$, so $\eta=T_{u,u}$. Applying this to $\sigma$ and to $\tau$ gives $\sigma=\tau=T_{u,u}=\rho$; hence every representation of $\rho$ as a nontrivial convex combination is trivial, and $\rho$ is an extreme point by [F6].

[(mixed $\Rightarrow$ not extreme) an explicit splitting] Assume now that $\rho$ is not pure. By [F1] the state $\rho$ has at least two positive eigenvalues; list them with multiplicity as $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ with orthonormal eigenvectors $u_1,u_2$, so $\lambda_2>0$. Put $\varepsilon:=\frac{\lambda_2}{2}>0,\qquad \sigma_\pm:=\rho\pm\varepsilon\bigl(T_{u_1,u_1}-T_{u_2,u_2}\bigr).$ The expansion of [F3] for $\rho$ turns the displayed definitions into countable mixtures of the pure states $T_{u_n,u_n}$ with weights $\lambda_1\pm\varepsilon$, $\lambda_2\mp\varepsilon$, $\lambda_3,\lambda_4,\dots$; these weights are nonnegative because $\lambda_2-\varepsilon=\varepsilon>0$ and $\lambda_1\pm\varepsilon\ge0$, and they sum to $\sum_n\lambda_n\pm\varepsilon\mp\varepsilon=1$; hence $\sigma_\pm\in D(H)$ by [F2]. Moreover $\rho=\tfrac12\sigma_++\tfrac12\sigma_-$, and $\sigma_+-\sigma_-=2\varepsilon(T_{u_1,u_1}-T_{u_2,u_2})$, which is nonzero because $u_1,u_2$ are orthogonal unit vectors and hence not phase multiples of one another, so that $T_{u_1,u_1}\ne T_{u_2,u_2}$ by [F5]. Thus the representation $\rho=\tfrac12\sigma_++\tfrac12\sigma_-$ with $\sigma_+\ne\sigma_-$ is a nontrivial convex representation with $0<\tfrac12<1$, and $\rho$ is not an extreme point by [F6].
[Conclusion] Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 show that every pure state is extreme, and step 4.1 shows that every non-pure state is not extreme. Hence the extreme points of $D(H)$ are exactly the pure states.

boundaries.reason: Only states and decompositions with 0<t<1 occur; no empty family is quantified over.

boundaries.evidence: The parameter t is restricted to 0<t<1 in the statement, and step 4.1 uses ε=λ2/2>0; zero or one values of t are excluded by the extremality condition itself, as recorded in step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: No singleton-index case occurs; the eigenvalue multiplicities in step 3.1 treat the single-eigenvalue case explicitly.
No degenerate limit occurs; the spectral expansion used in step 3.1 is over the finite-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces.

boundaries.evidence: The strict condition 0<t<1 is part of the statement and is what step 1.1 and step 4.1 use; t=0 and t=1 carry no information and are excluded.
The statement declares the Axiom of Countable Choice; the spectral and trace suppliers used in steps 3.1 and 4.1 assume it.
The direction pure ⟹ extreme is proved in steps 1.1-3.1.
The direction non-pure ⟹ not extreme (equivalently extreme ⟹ pure) is proved in steps 4.1-5.1.

citations.quote:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework, for systems in the declared massive-matter sector, the following statements about states and their composition. Assume throughout the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the mathematical suppliers cited below.

**(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

**(iii) General preparations and mixing.** A general preparation of the system is a **density operator**: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ on $H$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)). Pure preparations are the special case $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Every partial sum is positive; operator-norm convergence preserves its nonnegative quadratic forms, and continuity of trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. $$X:=\{\rho\in\mathcal S_1(H):\rho^{*}=\rho\}$$
for the set of self-adjoint trace-class operators, regarded as a real vector space by restricting scalars from $\mathbb C$ to $\mathbb R$ ([[lem-restriction-of-scalars]], [[def-subfield]]). Then:

(a) **Finite mixtures.** $X$ is a closed real-linear subspace of $\mathcal S_1(H)$ and hence a real Banach space, and $D(H)\subseteq X$ is **closed under finite real convex combinations**, that is, it contains with any two of its points the whole real segment between them: for all $\rho,\sigma\in D(H)$ and every real $\lambda\in[0,1]$,
$$\lambda\rho+(1-\lambda)\sigma\in D(H).$$
By induction every finite convex combination $\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_j\rho_j$ with $\rho_j\in D(H)$, real $\lambda_j\ge0$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j=1$ is again an element of $D(H)$.

(b) **Countable mixtures.** Let $(\rho_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq D(H)$ and let $(w_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be real weights with $w_n\ge0$ and $\sum_{n}w_n=1$. Then the series $\sum_{n}w_n\rho_n$ converges absolutely in $\|\cdot\|_1$ to an element of $D(H)$: the series converges in $X$, its sum $T$ satisfies $T^{*}=T$, $T\ge0$, $\operatorname{tr}T=1$, and $\|T\|_1=\operatorname{tr}T$, with
$$\Bigl\|T-\sum_{n<K}w_n\rho_n\Bigr\|_1\longrightarrow0\quad(K\to\infty).$$

(c) **Grouping of consecutive blocks.** In the situation of (b) let $0=N_0<N_1<N_2<\cdots$ be an increasing sequence with $N_k\to\infty$, and for every $k\in\mathbb N$ put
$$u_k:=\sum_{N_k\le n<N_{k+1}}w_n,\qquad \sigma_k:=\frac{1}{u_k}\sum_{N_k\le n<N_{k+1}}w_n\rho_n,$$
where it is assumed that $u_k>0$ for every $k$ (blocks of zero weight are omitted). Then $\sigma_k\in D(H)$ for every $k$, $\sum_ku_k=1$, and
$$\sum_{k}u_k\sigma_k=\sum_{n}w_n\rho_n$$
in $\|\cdot\|_1$, the series on the left converging absolutely.

(d) **Closedness and completeness.** $D(H)$ is closed in the Banach space $(X,\|\cdot\|_1)$, and $D(H)$ is complete for the trace-norm metric.

$$(\lambda_n)_{n\in J},\qquad J\ \text{a finite initial segment of}\ \mathbb N\ \text{or all of}\ \mathbb N,$$

([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
