**(b) Pure and mixed states.** A state is **pure** when it is one of the operators $T_{u,u}$ with $u\in S(H)$, and **mixed** when it is not pure, as in [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]. By [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] the map
$$j:R(H)\to D(H),\qquad j([\psi])=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
is a bijection of the ray space onto the set of pure states; and by clause (ii) of the state postulate the pure preparations are the unit rays of $H$, so the model's pure preparations are exactly its pure states.

**(c) State assigned to a state vector.** For a nonzero vector $\psi\in H^{\times}$ the **state assigned to $\psi$** is the normalized rank-one operator
$$\widehat\rho(\psi)=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)}\in D(H),$$
which by [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] depends only on the ray $[\psi]$; clause (ii) of the state postulate assigns the same operator to the pure preparation $[\psi]$. The zero vector is excluded here because $\|\psi\|^{-1}$ is defined only for $\psi\ne0$; no state is assigned to it, in agreement with the state postulate.

**(d) Mixtures and purity.** A **statistical mixture** of preparations with weights is the trace-norm convergent sum of clause (iii) of the state postulate; its value is the corresponding convex combination of states. The **purity** of a state $\rho$ is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})$, and by [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-purity-criterion]] a state is pure exactly when its purity equals $1$.

The cited mathematical suppliers of the ray-to-state correspondence and of the purity criterion assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is carried as a hypothesis of these readings. They adopt no assumption beyond the state postulate and that hypothesis, assert no dynamics, no probability law and no measurement model, and make no empirical claim: in particular, whether a given laboratory preparation is pure or mixed, and whether a given apparatus realizes a prescribed mixture, are physical identifications with uncertainty, governed by the preparation and apparatus assumptions of the framework, not consequences of this definition. Superselection restrictions and identical-particle symmetry sectors, where imposed, are separate assumptions by clause (v) of the state postulate and are not part of the state space fixed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $\rho\in D(H)$ be a density operator ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). Let
$$(\lambda_n)_{n\in J},\qquad J\ \text{a finite initial segment of}\ \mathbb N\ \text{or all of}\ \mathbb N,$$
be the positive eigenvalues of $\rho$ listed with multiplicity, so that $\rho=\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ for an orthonormal family $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ of eigenvectors, $\rho u_n=\lambda_nu_n$ ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]). Then:

(a) $\lambda_n>0$ for every $n\in J$, $\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n=1$, and $\lambda_n\le1$ for every $n\in J$.

(b) $\rho^{2}$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator, and its positive eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are exactly the numbers $\lambda_n^{2}$ with $n\in J$; consequently
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})=\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n^{2}\in(0,1].$$

(c) The following four statements are equivalent: (i) $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})=1$; (ii) $J=\{n_0\}$ for a single index $n_0$ and $\lambda_{n_0}=1$; (iii) $\rho$ is a pure state; (iv) $\rho^{2}=\rho$.

(d) If $\rho$ is not pure, then $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})<1$ and $J$ contains at least two indices, so that $\rho$ has at least two positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, which is the choice hypothesis of the rank-one calculus [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$$T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u\qquad(x\in H)$$
be the rank-one operator calculus of that item. Use the notation of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]] for the unit sphere $S(H)$, the nonzero vectors $H^{\times}$, the ray $[\psi]$, the ray space $R(H)$ and the normalization $\nu$. Then:

(a) For every $\psi\in H^{\times}$ the operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ is a nonzero self-adjoint positive trace-class operator with
$$\|T_{\psi,\psi}\|_1=\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})=\|\psi\|^{2},\qquad T_{\psi,\psi}=\|\psi\|^{2}\,T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},\qquad \langle T_{\psi,\psi}x,x\rangle=|\langle x,\psi\rangle|^{2}\quad(x\in H).$$

(b) For every $u\in S(H)$ the operator $T_{u,u}$ is the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto the one-dimensional linear subspace $\mathbb Cu$; in particular $T_{u,u}\ne0$, $T_{u,u}^{2}=T_{u,u}$ and $T_{u,u}^{*}=T_{u,u}$. Conversely, if $M$ is a one-dimensional linear subspace of $H$ and $u\in S(H)$ satisfies $M=\mathbb Cu$, then the Hilbert orthogonal projection $P_M$ onto $M$ equals $T_{u,u}$. Thus the operators $T_{u,u}$ with $u\in S(H)$ are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range.

(c) For nonzero $\psi,\varphi\in H^{\times}$:
$$T_{\psi,\psi}=T_{\varphi,\varphi}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \|\psi\|=\|\varphi\|\ \text{and}\ [\psi]=[\varphi].$$
In particular, for $u,w\in S(H)$ one has $T_{u,u}=T_{w,w}$ if and only if $w=\zeta u$ for some $\zeta\in U(1)$.

(d) The map
$$j:R(H)\longrightarrow \mathcal S_1(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
is well defined and injective, and its image is exactly $\{T_{u,u}:u\in S(H)\}$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

### The span

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be self-adjoint
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). Then:

1. every eigenvalue of $T$
   ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) is a real number:
   if $Tx=\lambda x$ with $x\ne0$, then $\lambda\in\mathbb R$;
2. eigenspaces belonging to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal: if
   $\lambda\ne\mu$ and $x\in E_\lambda(T)$, $y\in E_\mu(T)$, then
   $\langle x,y\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $D(H)$ be the state space of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]. Write $\mathcal S_1(H)$ for the complex Banach space of trace-class operators on $H$ with the trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$, and
$$X:=\{\rho\in\mathcal S_1(H):\rho^{*}=\rho\}$$
for the set of self-adjoint trace-class operators, regarded as a real vector space by restricting scalars from $\mathbb C$ to $\mathbb R$ ([[lem-restriction-of-scalars]], [[def-subfield]]). Then:

(a) **Finite mixtures.** $X$ is a closed real-linear subspace of $\mathcal S_1(H)$ and hence a real Banach space, and $D(H)\subseteq X$ is **closed under finite real convex combinations**, that is, it contains with any two of its points the whole real segment between them: for all $\rho,\sigma\in D(H)$ and every real $\lambda\in[0,1]$,
$$\lambda\rho+(1-\lambda)\sigma\in D(H).$$
By induction every finite convex combination $\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_j\rho_j$ with $\rho_j\in D(H)$, real $\lambda_j\ge0$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j=1$ is again an element of $D(H)$.

(b) **Countable mixtures.** Let $(\rho_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq D(H)$ and let $(w_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be real weights with $w_n\ge0$ and $\sum_{n}w_n=1$. $$\Bigl\|T-\sum_{n<K}w_n\rho_n\Bigr\|_1\longrightarrow0\quad(K\to\infty).$$

where it is assumed that $u_k>0$ for every $k$ (blocks of zero weight are omitted). Then $\sigma_k\in D(H)$ for every $k$, $\sum_ku_k=1$, and
$$\sum_{k}u_k\sigma_k=\sum_{n}w_n\rho_n$$

$$X:=\{\rho\in\mathcal S_1(H):\rho^{*}=\rho\}$$
for the set of self-adjoint trace-class operators, regarded as a real vector space by restricting scalars from $\mathbb C$ to $\mathbb R$ ([[lem-restriction-of-scalars]], [[def-subfield]]). Then:

(a) **Finite mixtures.** $X$ is a closed real-linear subspace of $\mathcal S_1(H)$ and hence a real Banach space, and $D(H)\subseteq X$ is **closed under finite real convex combinations**, that is, it contains with any two of its points the whole real segment between them: for all $\rho,\sigma\in D(H)$ and every real $\lambda\in[0,1]$,
$$\lambda\rho+(1-\lambda)\sigma\in D(H).$$
By induction every finite convex combination $\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_j\rho_j$ with $\rho_j\in D(H)$, real $\lambda_j\ge0$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j=1$ is again an element of $D(H)$.

(b) **Countable mixtures.** Let $(\rho_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq D(H)$ and let $(w_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be real weights with $w_n\ge0$ and $\sum_{n}w_n=1$. Then the series $\sum_{n}w_n\rho_n$ converges absolutely in $\|\cdot\|_1$ to an element of $D(H)$: the series converges in $X$, its sum $T$ satisfies $T^{*}=T$, $T\ge0$, $\operatorname{tr}T=1$, and $\|T\|_1=\operatorname{tr}T$, with
$$\Bigl\|T-\sum_{n<K}w_n\rho_n\Bigr\|_1\longrightarrow0\quad(K\to\infty).$$

(c) **Grouping of consecutive blocks.** In the situation of (b) let $0=N_0<N_1<N_2<\cdots$ be an increasing sequence with $N_k\to\infty$, and for every $k\in\mathbb N$ put
$$u_k:=\sum_{N_k\le n<N_{k+1}}w_n,\qquad \sigma_k:=\frac{1}{u_k}\sum_{N_k\le n<N_{k+1}}w_n\rho_n,$$
where it is assumed that $u_k>0$ for every $k$ (blocks of zero weight are omitted). Then $\sigma_k\in D(H)$ for every $k$, $\sum_ku_k=1$, and
$$\sum_{k}u_k\sigma_k=\sum_{n}w_n\rho_n$$
in $\|\cdot\|_1$, the series on the left converging absolutely.

(d) **Closedness and completeness.** $D(H)$ is closed in the Banach space $(X,\|\cdot\|_1)$, and $D(H)$ is complete for the trace-norm metric.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $\rho\in D(H)$ be a density operator ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). Let
$$(\lambda_n)_{n\in J},\qquad J\ \text{a finite initial segment of}\ \mathbb N\ \text{or all of}\ \mathbb N,$$
be the positive eigenvalues of $\rho$ listed with multiplicity, so that $\rho=\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ for an orthonormal family $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ of eigenvectors, $\rho u_n=\lambda_nu_n$ ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]). Then:

(a) $\lambda_n>0$ for every $n\in J$, $\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n=1$, and $\lambda_n\le1$ for every $n\in J$.

(b) $\rho^{2}$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator, and its positive eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are exactly the numbers $\lambda_n^{2}$ with $n\in J$; consequently
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})=\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n^{2}\in(0,1].$$

(c) The following four statements are equivalent: (i) $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})=1$; (ii) $J=\{n_0\}$ for a single index $n_0$ and $\lambda_{n_0}=1$; (iii) $\rho$ is a pure state; (iv) $\rho^{2}=\rho$.

(d) If $\rho$ is not pure, then $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})<1$ and $J$ contains at least two indices, so that $\rho$ has at least two positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.

Adopt the state and composition postulate P1 of the framework ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]]) and use the state-space vocabulary of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the spectral and mixture suppliers cited below. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be the Hilbert space assigned to a declared system. Then:

(a) **Mixtures.** Let $(\rho_n)$ be a finite or countable family of preparations with real weights $w_n\ge0$ satisfying $\sum_nw_n=1$. Then the statistical mixture $\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ of clause (iii) of P1 converges in trace norm to a preparation, namely to the density operator $T=\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ of [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-density-set-convex-and-complete]]. The mixture is affine in its data: a term of zero weight may be added or removed without changing $T$, and splitting one weight between two copies of the same preparation, $w\rho=w_1\rho+w_2\rho$ with $w_1+w_2=w$, leaves $T$ unchanged. If the index set is partitioned into consecutive finite blocks with total weights $u_k>0$ and block mixtures $\sigma_k$, then $\sum_ku_k\sigma_k=\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ in trace norm, so mixtures may be regrouped.

(b) **Spectral decomposition.** Every preparation $\rho$ is a countable statistical mixture of pairwise orthogonal pure preparations: there exist a finite or countable orthonormal family $(u_n)$ of unit vectors and positive weights $\lambda_n$ with $\sum_n\lambda_n=1$ such that
$$\rho=\sum_n\lambda_n\,T_{u_n,u_n},$$
the sum converging in trace norm, and the weights $\lambda_n$ are exactly the positive eigenvalues of $\rho$ counted with multiplicity.

(c) **Extremality and nontrivial decompositions.** A preparation is pure if and only if its density operator is an extreme point of the state space $D(H)$ in the sense of the condition displayed in [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-extreme-points-of-the-state-space]]; consequently every mixed preparation $\rho$ admits a representation as a statistical mixture of two preparations in a nontrivial way: if $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2>0$ are two positive eigenvalues of $\rho$ with orthonormal eigenvectors $u_1$ and $u_2$, then with $\varepsilon:=\lambda_2/2$ the operators
$$\sigma_\pm:=\rho\pm\varepsilon\bigl(T_{u_1,u_1}-T_{u_2,u_2}\bigr)$$
are preparations with $\rho=\tfrac12\sigma_++\tfrac12\sigma_-$ and $\sigma_+\ne\sigma_-$.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework, for systems in the declared massive-matter sector, the following statements about states and their composition. Assume throughout the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the mathematical suppliers cited below.

**(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

**(iii) General preparations and mixing.** A general preparation of the system is a **density operator**: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ on $H$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)). Pure preparations are the special case $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Every partial sum is positive; operator-norm convergence preserves its nonnegative quadratic forms, and continuity of trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. Distinct weighted ensembles of pure states may define the same $\rho$.

**(iv) Composition.** Two independent distinguishable subsystems with state spaces $H_{A}$ and $H_{B}$ are composed by the completed Hilbert tensor product $H_{A}\widehat\otimes H_{B}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]. Product preparations $\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B}$ are the special case of preparations in which each subsystem has its own specified preparation; general composite preparations are linear combinations and mixtures and need not factor. A quantity of subsystem $A$ alone is represented on the composite by an operator of the form $A\otimes I_{B}$ and a quantity of $B$ alone by $I_{A}\otimes B$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] (bounded case; unbounded local operators are treated where they occur). The existence of the completed tensor product is mathematics; the assignment of that product to a composite physical system is the physical assumption here.

**(v) Restrictions that are separate assumptions.** Restrictions of the state space by superselection rules, identical-particle symmetry sectors, and the replacement of the tensor product by more general algebraic structures are not consequences of the clauses above: where such a restriction is used it is adopted separately, and the identical-species sectors are the subject of the postulate P6 of this page.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model within its declared sector. They are not derived from experiment, and they do not assert that a physical system is exactly described by such a Hilbert space; no numerical measurement is recorded. The compatibility of the framework with observation is a question about fully specified models and reported data, in the sense of P7.

**The Hilbert space and its norm.** Throughout this item $H\ne\{0\}$ is a nonzero complex Hilbert space, with pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and with the induced norm $\|\psi\|:=\sqrt{\langle\psi,\psi\rangle}$ ([[def-inner-product-norm]], [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]). A **vector** is an element of $H$, and a **unit vector** is a vector $\psi$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. The **unit sphere** of $H$ is
$$S(H):=\{\psi\in H:\|\psi\|=1\},$$
and the set of **nonzero vectors** is $H^{\times}:=H\setminus\{0\}$. The hypothesis $H\ne\{0\}$ says exactly that $H^{\times}$ is nonempty; then $S(H)$ is nonempty as well, since for every nonzero $\psi$ the vector $\psi/\|\psi\|$ has norm one, because $\|\psi\|>0$ and $\|\psi/\|\psi\|\,\|=|\|\psi\|^{-1}|\,\|\psi\|=1$.

**Rays.** For $\psi\in H^{\times}$ the **ray** of $\psi$ is
$$[\psi]:=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C,\ z\ne0\}\subseteq H^{\times}.$$
A **ray** of $H$ is a subset of the form $[\psi]$ for some nonzero $\psi$, and an element of a ray is called a **representative** of it. The set of rays
$$R(H):=\{[\psi]:\psi\in H^{\times}\}$$
is the **ray space** of $H$. Two nonzero vectors $\psi,\varphi$ are **ray-equivalent** when they lie in a common ray, that is, when $\varphi=z\psi$ for some nonzero complex number $z$. Ray equivalence is an equivalence relation on $H^{\times}$: it is reflexive with $z=1$, symmetric with $z^{-1}$, and transitive by multiplying scalars. Its classes are exactly the rays, so $R(H)$ is the quotient set of $H^{\times}$ by this relation, and every nonzero vector lies in exactly one ray.

**Normalization.** The **normalization map** is
$$\nu:H^{\times}\longrightarrow S(H),\qquad \nu(\psi):=\frac{\psi}{\|\psi\|},$$
where the right-hand side is the scalar multiple $\|\psi\|^{-1}\psi$; the displayed definition is meaningful because $\|\psi\|>0$ for $\psi\ne0$. The vector $\nu(\psi)$ is the **normalization** of $\psi$.

**Phases.** The **phase group** is
$$U(1):=\{\zeta\in\mathbb C:|\zeta|=1\}$$
([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]), and a **phase factor** is an element of $U(1)$. Two vectors $\psi,\varphi$ are **phase-equivalent** when $\varphi=\zeta\psi$ for some phase factor $\zeta$. The **phase action** of $U(1)$ on the unit sphere is the map
$$U(1)\times S(H)\longrightarrow S(H),\qquad (\zeta,\psi)\longmapsto\zeta\psi,$$
which is well defined because $\|\zeta\psi\|=|\zeta|\,\|\psi\|=\|\psi\|$ for $\zeta\in U(1)$ and $\psi\in S(H)$. Ray equivalence allows multiplication by an arbitrary nonzero complex scalar, while phase equivalence allows multiplication by a scalar of modulus one only; within a given ray the two notions coincide exactly on representatives of equal norm, and the precise statements are proved in the normalization lemma of this page.

**Scope.** This definition fixes the mathematical objects of the state space of a Hilbert space and their elementary vocabulary: nonzero vectors, unit vectors, rays, the ray space, the normalization map and the phase action. It introduces no topology or measure on $R(H)$, no dynamics and no physical interpretation, and it uses no choice principle. The identification of rays with preparations and of the unit sphere with their normalized representatives is the model assumption stated in the framework's state postulate, not part of this mathematical definition; the orbit structure of the phase action is analysed in the normalization lemma of this page.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, which is the choice hypothesis of the rank-one calculus [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$$T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u\qquad(x\in H)$$
be the rank-one operator calculus of that item. Use the notation of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]] for the unit sphere $S(H)$, the nonzero vectors $H^{\times}$, the ray $[\psi]$, the ray space $R(H)$ and the normalization $\nu$. Then:

(a) For every $\psi\in H^{\times}$ the operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ is a nonzero self-adjoint positive trace-class operator with
$$\|T_{\psi,\psi}\|_1=\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})=\|\psi\|^{2},\qquad T_{\psi,\psi}=\|\psi\|^{2}\,T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},\qquad \langle T_{\psi,\psi}x,x\rangle=|\langle x,\psi\rangle|^{2}\quad(x\in H).$$

(b) For every $u\in S(H)$ the operator $T_{u,u}$ is the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto the one-dimensional linear subspace $\mathbb Cu$; in particular $T_{u,u}\ne0$, $T_{u,u}^{2}=T_{u,u}$ and $T_{u,u}^{*}=T_{u,u}$. Conversely, if $M$ is a one-dimensional linear subspace of $H$ and $u\in S(H)$ satisfies $M=\mathbb Cu$, then the Hilbert orthogonal projection $P_M$ onto $M$ equals $T_{u,u}$. Thus the operators $T_{u,u}$ with $u\in S(H)$ are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range.

(c) For nonzero $\psi,\varphi\in H^{\times}$:
$$T_{\psi,\psi}=T_{\varphi,\varphi}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \|\psi\|=\|\varphi\|\ \text{and}\ [\psi]=[\varphi].$$
In particular, for $u,w\in S(H)$ one has $T_{u,u}=T_{w,w}$ if and only if $w=\zeta u$ for some $\zeta\in U(1)$.

(d) The map
$$j:R(H)\longrightarrow \mathcal S_1(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
is well defined and injective, and its image is exactly $\{T_{u,u}:u\in S(H)\}$.

A **field** is a set $F$ equipped with two binary operations $+$ (addition) and
$\cdot$ (multiplication) and two distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$ of $F$,
satisfying:

- **(A)** $(F, +)$ is an abelian group with identity $0$: addition is
  associative and commutative, $x + 0 = x$ for all $x$, and every $x$ has an
  additive inverse $-x$ with $x + (-x) = 0$.
- **(M)** Multiplication is associative and commutative **on all of $F$**, and
  $x \cdot 1 = x$ for every $x \in F$; moreover $(F \setminus \{0\}, \cdot)$ is an
  abelian group with identity $1$, so every $x \ne 0$ has a multiplicative inverse
  $x^{-1}$ with $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$.
- **(D)** Multiplication distributes over addition: $x \cdot (y + z) = x\cdot y + x\cdot z$.

We write $x - y := x + (-y)$ and $x/y := x \cdot y^{-1}$ (for $y \ne 0$), and
abbreviate $x \cdot y$ as $xy$.

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

derivations.claim: [No unit representative] By [L2], $\|0\|=0$ and $\|z\cdot0\|=|z|\,\|0\|=0$ for every scalar $z$, so no scalar multiple of $0$ has norm $1$; hence the set $\{z\cdot0:z\ne0\}=\{0\}$ contains no unit vector, and it is not a ray in the sense of [L2], which is defined only for nonzero generating vectors.

[Normalization is undefined] The normalization formula $\nu(\psi)=\|\psi\|^{-1}\psi$ uses the inverse of the scalar $\|\psi\|$; at $\psi=0$ this inverse would be $0^{-1}$, which does not exist in $\mathbb C$ by [L4], and the displayed "convention" $0/\|0\|=0$ is therefore not an instance of the definition but a separate stipulation. Even granting the stipulation its value, $\|0\|=0\ne1$ by [L2], so it does not produce a unit representative; the stipulation is self-defeating as a normalization rule.

[The zero operator is not a state] By [L3], $T_{0,0}$ is the zero operator with $\operatorname{tr}(T_{0,0})=0$; a density operator has trace one by [L1], so $0\notin D(H)$ and the zero operator is not a state of the model. Consequently the zero vector does not determine a state through the rank-one operator either.

[Failure at every step] The refuted statement fails on the zero vector in all of its assertions: there is no unit representative of $0$ by step 1.1, the normalization is undefined rather than $0$ by step 2.1, and the zero operator is not a density operator by step 2.2; and clause (ii) of the state postulate in [L1] expressly assigns no preparation to the zero vector. Hence the claim that every vector of the assigned Hilbert space determines a pure preparation, with the zero vector as the state of an empty preparation, is refuted.
